bicep-first-words.focus: Find param greeting string and output message string in the picture. param accepts a value; output describes a returned value.
bicep-first-words.why: Follow one input into one output.
bicep-first-words.proof: In generated JSON, expand parameters → greeting and find defaultValue: Hello, learner. Find outputs → message and confirm that it refers to greeting.
bicep-first-words.scenario: At work, a reusable blueprint accepts a different application name for each team.

bicep-workspace.focus: Read the displayed PowerShell prompt. PS names the shell; the path is the current folder; > marks where your input begins. Type only the command after >.
bicep-workspace.why: The current folder selects the file.
bicep-workspace.proof: In VS Code → Terminal, type Get-Location and press Enter. Confirm the path ends in CloudSeam-Bicep; in Explorer, confirm the file is main.bicep, not main.bicep.txt.
bicep-workspace.scenario: At work, two folders may each contain main.bicep. Checking your folder prevents building the wrong file.

bicep-toolchain.focus: Identify three separate tools: VS Code edits the file, the Microsoft Bicep extension explains its language, and az bicep compiles saved files.
bicep-toolchain.proof: In your practice-folder PowerShell, type az bicep version and record the version. Build main.bicep, then open main.json in VS Code’s Explorer and find parameters and outputs.
bicep-toolchain.scenario: At work, record the compiler version so a teammate can reproduce your build.

bicep-errors.focus: Find the single quote on each side of the greeting text. These quotes mark the beginning and end of a text value.
bicep-errors.why: Repair the first reported error first.
bicep-errors.proof: Compile after restoring the missing quote. Confirm that the quote error is gone and generated ARM JSON is available; save the error and repair in your notebook.
bicep-errors.scenario: At work, one missing quote can produce several diagnostics. Fixing the first often clears the others.

bicep-inputs.focus: Find environment and resourceName. You choose environment: it is the independent input. resourceName uses that input: it is the dependent value. var declares a calculated or reusable value; it is not automatically independent.
bicep-inputs.why: Change the input; trace its effect.
bicep-inputs.proof: In generated JSON, find environment.defaultValue and confirm test. Find the expression that builds app- from environment. Explain why ARM, not this compile step, resolves deployment-time expressions.
bicep-inputs.scenario: At work, the same blueprint can plan app-dev and app-test by changing one environment input.

bicep-types.focus: Find string, int, bool, array and object in the example. They mean text, whole number, true/false, ordered list and named fields.
bicep-types.why: A value must match its type.
bicep-types.proof: In generated JSON → parameters, confirm serverCount is int, enableFeature is bool and teams is array. Confirm the values are 3, true and your three team names.
bicep-types.scenario: At work, a server count must be a number, while a team name is text.

bicep-resource.focus: Read resource storage from left to right: storage is your local symbolic name; Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts is the Azure resource type; the @ value selects an API contract.
bicep-resource.why: Know which setting you are changing.
bicep-resource.proof: After restoring Standard_LRS, compile again. In generated JSON → resources → the storage account → sku → name, confirm Standard_LRS.
bicep-resource.scenario: At work, changing a storage redundancy setting affects cost and resilience; compilation is not a cost estimate.

bicep-json.focus: Compare the source and generated JSON pictures. Bicep is the readable authoring language; ARM JSON is the translated template, not a log of created resources.
bicep-json.proof: Find the storage account in resources. Match its type, apiVersion, sku.name and properties to the Bicep declaration. Write one matching pair in your notebook.
bicep-json.scenario: At work, inspect a generated template when a build behaves differently from what the author intended.

bicep-guards.focus: Find @minValue, @maxValue and @secure. Decorators add rules to the declaration below them; @secure does not make a hard-coded secret safe to publish.
bicep-guards.proof: Restore serverCount to 2 and compile. Confirm the constraint error is gone and adminPassword is secureString in generated JSON. Keep real passwords out of this exercise.
bicep-guards.scenario: At work, a count limit can prevent a typo from requesting hundreds of servers.

bicep-dependencies.focus: Find nsg.id inside the subnet. The subnet configuration depends on the NSG. This is a resource dependency, different from a calculated value depending on an input.
bicep-dependencies.proof: In generated JSON, find the VNet resource’s dependency on the NSG. Write: NSG → subnet configuration. Two unrelated resources can deploy in parallel; their position in the file is not an ordering instruction.
bicep-dependencies.scenario: At work, an application VM needs its NIC, and that NIC needs its subnet. References express this order.

bicep-network.focus: Find the VNet, apps subnet and NSG. A VNet is the private network, a subnet is a section of it, and an NSG filters traffic using rules.
bicep-network.why: Placement and access are separate decisions.
bicep-network.proof: In Resource declarations in this template, identify the NSG and VNet. In the subnet properties, find the NSG reference. Explain why a deny rule does not create a reachable website.
bicep-network.scenario: At work, application and database servers may use different subnets and different permitted traffic.

bicep-existing.focus: Find existing in the NSG declaration. This tells Bicep to reference a resource managed elsewhere rather than request a new one.
bicep-existing.proof: Compile with your dummy existingNsgName. Find the changed parameter default and confirm the existing NSG is not a new resource creation entry. Record: existence was not checked against Azure.
bicep-existing.scenario: At work, a network team may own the NSG while your team owns the application blueprint.

bicep-loops.focus: Find range(0, serverCount). With a count of 3, i takes 0, 1 and 2. The count is your input; each generated instance and its name depend on that input and index.
bicep-loops.why: Repeat a plan without duplicating it.
bicep-loops.proof: In generated JSON, find both copy blocks and the serverCount parameter. Trace nics[i].id to the VM at the same index. Record three planned VM instances, not three deployed VMs.
bicep-loops.scenario: At work, a team may need three identical application servers with distinct names and NICs.

bicep-server-settings.focus: Find imageReference, vmSize, osDisk and osProfile. They describe the operating system image, compute size, boot disk and guest sign-in settings.
bicep-server-settings.why: Plan the server before creating it.
bicep-server-settings.proof: In generated JSON, find the VM size, image publisher/offer/sku, managed disk type and disablePasswordAuthentication. Explain which fields you would review for an application’s requirements.
bicep-server-settings.scenario: At work, an application may need more memory while retaining the same approved OS image and sign-in policy.

bicep-software.focus: Find loadTextContent('cloud-init.yml'). The template reads a companion file; a future Linux VM uses its contents during first-boot configuration.
bicep-software.why: Infrastructure and guest setup work together.
bicep-software.proof: Compile with cloud-init.yml present. Find the VM’s customData expression in generated JSON. Record that neither the VM nor NGINX has run during compilation.
bicep-software.scenario: At work, a new Linux application server may need NGINX installed consistently on its first boot.

bicep-modules.focus: Find module network './network.bicep'. The parent supplies the module’s inputs; network.outputs.subnetId reads a result from that module.
bicep-modules.why: Reuse a tested part of the plan.
bicep-modules.proof: In generated JSON, find the nested deployment and its parameters. Trace the prefix input into the network module and its subnetId output back to the parent.
bicep-modules.scenario: At work, several applications can reuse a network module instead of maintaining separate copies.

bicep-environments.focus: Read using './main.bicep' and param environment = 'dev'. The blueprint stays the same; the parameter file supplies environment-specific inputs.
bicep-environments.why: Separate the blueprint from its inputs.
bicep-environments.proof: In VS Code, compare dev.json and test.json generated by build-params. Confirm their environment values differ while both parameter files point to the same main.bicep.
bicep-environments.scenario: At work, development and test can share a blueprint while using different approved names and counts.

bicep-azure-checks.focus: Distinguish compile, validate and what-if. Compile translates the file; live validation checks it against Azure; what-if previews expected changes. None is a completed deployment.
bicep-azure-checks.why: Use the right evidence for each claim.
bicep-azure-checks.proof: Save the compiler result. If you performed the optional live checks, record the approved scope and actual validation/what-if result separately. Otherwise write Live checks: not run.
bicep-azure-checks.scenario: At work, a syntactically valid VM plan can still fail because of policy, permissions, quota or region availability.

bicep-capstone.focus: Read the requested plan: private application servers, an NSG, one VNet/apps subnet, NICs and SSH-key sign-in. Identify inputs before writing resource declarations.
bicep-capstone.why: Break a real request into small parts.
bicep-capstone.proof: Compile your own attempt. Trace NSG → subnet → NIC → VM references, then compare your count and security settings with the requirements. Record any missing requirement even if compilation passes.
bicep-capstone.scenario: At work, a request for three application servers becomes a reviewed blueprint, not a rush to create machines manually.

bicep-handoff.focus: Read CI as automatic checks on a proposed change. Read CD as a controlled delivery/deployment stage after those checks. A green build is not proof of a secure running server.
bicep-handoff.proof: Complete the CI security mini-lab linked below. Record the failed build caused by an intentionally unused input, then the successful build after its removal. Keep this separate from any Azure deployment evidence.
bicep-handoff.scenario: At work, a pull request is checked before approval, and deployment uses a separate, restricted identity.
